proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus (ius abutendi) is one of the three classical Roman-law incidents of dominium (usus, fructus, abusus). It is the power of the owner to alienate, consume, destroy, or otherwise dispose of a thing. Like LegalRight in the working ontology, it is a Role (BFO_0000023): it is externally grounded in a legal system that recognizes dominium, it inheres in a legal person (the owner), and it is realized in acts of disposal. It is a kind-level entity (a class) because any owner of property bears an instance of it. Subclassing under working:LegalRight is appropriate since LegalRight is already typed as BFO_0000023.

entities.label: ActOfDisposal
entities.rationale: Abusus as a realizable entity (Role) is realized in concrete acts of disposal — alienation, destruction, consumption of the thing. These are processes (BFO_0000015). Minting ActOfDisposal as the canonical realization process class allows the BFO_0000054 (realized in) relation to be stated. This class may also be useful for other disposition/right realization analyses.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a species of legal right (specifically an ownership incident conferring disposal power), so it subclasses the working:LegalRight Role class.

BFO realizes-in: an instance of Abusus (the role) is realized in an instance of ActOfDisposal (a process of alienating, consuming, or destroying the thing). At the class level this is stated as a domain-range constraint / OWL subclass axiom: Abusus subClassOf realized-in some ActOfDisposal.
ActOfDisposal is a kind of process (BFO_0000015), explicitly grounding it in BFO.

open_questions: Should Abusus be modeled as an individual (the specific Roman-law concept named 'Abusus') rather than a class, given that the user asked to 'classify' it — implying kind-level treatment is preferred? The current proposal treats it as a class (kind) because multiple owners each bear their own instance.

The classical Roman triad also includes Usus (right of use) and Fructus (right to fruits). Should these be minted as sibling subclasses of LegalRight now for completeness, or deferred to a later utterance?

Abusus inheres in a material-entity bearer (the legal person / owner). Should we also assert a domain restriction: Abusus RO_0000052 inheres-in some LegalPerson — and if so, should LegalPerson be minted as a working class (subclass of BFO_0000040)?

Is the target ontology concerned with Roman law historically (in which case Abusus might also need a temporal-region qualifier) or with the abstract doctrinal concept as used in comparative property law today?
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus (ius abutendi) in Roman-law property theory names the owner's power of disposal over a thing — to alienate, consume, or destroy it. In BFO terms it is best typed as a Role (BFO_0000023): it is an externally grounded, specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the bearer (the legal person recognized as dominus by the legal system), and it is not an intrinsic quality of the person but depends on the existence of the legal system's recognition of dominium. Because every owner of a corporeal thing bears their own numerically distinct instance of this power, Abusus is appropriately a class (kind), not an individual. It is placed as a subclass of the existing working:LegalRight class (itself already typed BFO_0000023). Its realization is an ActOfDisposal (BFO_0000015 Process) — the concrete event of sale, gift, destruction, etc. — connected via BFO's realized-in (BFO_0000054) relation. This models the classical metaphysics precisely: the right persists as a continuant until exercised (realized) in a process.
